info.title: Hanzo Cloud API
info.description: Package platform is Hanzo PaaS: deploy containers to your own tenant namespace — builds, releases, environments, logs, custom domains.

post.summary: Triggers a native build — an image, or the binaries a repo declares.
post.description:
Triggers a native build — an image, or the binaries a repo declares.

The fabric's own build trigger, and what `hanzo build` and git-push-to-deploy
call. It answers 202 with the build job id: a queued build, not a pushed
artifact.

Two lanes, and a build is exactly one of them. The IMAGE lane takes `repo` and
the output `image` and launches a BuildKit Job that pushes it. The ARTIFACT lane
takes `binaries` — the same recipe the repo's hanzo.yml declares — and publishes
to object storage instead; it must carry no `image`, because a build produces
binaries or an image, never both.

PRIVILEGED, and A BUILD BELONGS TO THE ORGANIZATION ITS CREDENTIAL NAMES. Two
credentials, never a third:

  - one that NAMES an organization — a person who administers it (the `hanzo
    build` path, so one IAM login authorizes a build with no separate build
    token), or that organization's own machine identity (the pipeline path). The
    build is attributed to that org and confined to what it owns.
  - the shared build-callback token, compared in constant time. It names NO
    organization, which is both why the fabric's own release can publish across
    brands with it and why anything that CAN name one is read first.

Both are bounded by the owned-registry allowlist. The org path is bounded again,
by the org: the image's registry namespace must be one that organization owns, so
it publishes into its own brand and can never overwrite another's through the
shared push credential. The same confinement applies to the artifact lane's repo
owner. There is no request field naming an organization — the attribution is read
off the credential, so there is nothing for a caller to write it with.

The output image is parsed and validated as a single well-formed OCI ref before
any authorization decision reads it, so a crafted ref cannot smuggle a
build-exporter attribute past the check.

get.summary: Answers one build: its status, and for a failed build the reason.
get.description:
Answers one build: its status, and for a failed build the reason.

A build belongs to the organization its credential names, so it is read by the
credential that could have asked for it, and another organization's build is
404 rather than 403: whether an id exists is not said to anyone it is not for.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: ID is the build's id, from the path.

get.summary: Answers one build's BuildKit output: the log of each Job that ran it, every container in the order it ran them, so a failed step's real error is readable rather than cut off at the RUN line that failed.
get.description:
Answers one build's BuildKit output: the log of each Job that ran
it, every container in the order it ran them, so a failed step's real error is
readable rather than cut off at the RUN line that failed.

The log is read from the cluster when asked, never stored, so it lives as long
as the build's pods do: once their TTL reaps them `log` is empty, and the status
and reason GET /v1/build/{id} answers are what remain.

A build belongs to the organization its credential names, and another
organization's build is 404, exactly as GET /v1/build/{id} answers it.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: ID is the build's id, from the path.

get.summary: Answers what this organisation has declared, joined with what the delivery plane has done about it.
get.description:
Answers what this organisation has declared, joined with what
the delivery plane has done about it.

The join is best-effort BY DESIGN and says so when it is missing: the
declarations ARE the answer to "what have I deployed", so refusing the whole
board because the cluster is unreadable would lose the half that is readable.
What must never happen is a silent null — an unreadable plane is reported as
`cd.unavailable` carrying the reason, never as an app with no reconciliation,
and a values file that does not parse is listed in `unreadable`, never dropped.

parameters.name: org
parameters.description:
Org names the organisation whose declarations to read, defaulting to the
caller's own. Only a SuperAdmin may name one that is not theirs; anyone
else naming a foreign org is refused, so this widens nothing by itself.

post.description:
Builds a git repository into an image and writes the declaration that names it — a values file in `hanzoai/universe` under `charts/app/values/<namespace>/<name>.yaml`, which the `fleet` ApplicationSet renders as one Application. That file IS the deployment: nothing else has to be applied.

`repo` is a GitHub repository — `owner/name` or `https://github.com/owner/name` — or another https clone URL. A GitHub repository must be one the caller may see: their own connected GitHub, or the installations their org holds for an org admin (the same set `GET /v1/provider/github/repos` lists); anything else is 404. It is built at the name GitHub gives it now, from `ref`, which defaults to its default branch. This deployment's own git address naming an owner other than the caller's org (`https://<api host>/v1/git/<owner>/<name>.git`, as the builder sends a GitHub repository) is read as that GitHub repository. A private GitHub repository built for an org outside the estate is handed a token that reads that one repository, for an hour at most, minted as the caller: their own GitHub must push to it, or they administer the org whose installation reaches it. A caller GitHub mints no token for is refused before anything is built. Any other URL is an org admin's to build.

`partOf` names the project the app belongs to, and defaults to the app's own name.

Every member of the org may deploy; WHERE it lands is the difference. An org admin commits to universe main and CD applies it — in one call, naming the tag its own build will push, which CD pulls once the build lands. Anyone else opens a review: the declaration is pushed to `deploy/<namespace>/<name>/<tag>`, `declaration.review` is the link that opens the pull request, and nothing deploys until it is merged. `mode` may say `branch` to make an admin's deploy a review too; a non-admin naming `commit` is refused, never downgraded.

A member's deploy is bounded by who asked: ten deploys an hour and five open review branches. Past a bound it answers 429. A review branch is deleted once main declares its tag, or after seven days unmerged; `notice` says so, and that the public `env` values the branch carries are cleartext in universe, where deleting the branch does not unpublish them.

A release of an image an earlier call built (`tag` given) is proven pullable before main is pointed at it — a declaration naming an image the registry cannot serve is an ImagePullBackOff with no rollback path.

Omit `tag` to build; give it to declare an image an earlier call already built, which is how a green build is released without rebuilding it. That release is an org admin's: a member's deploy always builds, and carries public `env` only — a sealed value would write the running app's secrets before the review is merged, so a member naming one is refused.

An org is its name: the values DIRECTORY, the destination NAMESPACE and the AppProject FENCE are all `<org>`, and the image is `<registry>/<org>/<app>`. None of them is a request field — the directory decides what CD admits the sync under and the repository decides what the cluster pulls, so a caller who could name either could reach outside its own org.

`org` is an ACT-AS, not a placement field: it defaults to the caller's own, and naming another requires SuperAdmin. So does naming a RESERVED org — the platform's own namespace family (the brands and their environments, the control and delivery planes, `admin`) — even when it is the caller's own, because an IAM org named `kube-system` does not own Kubernetes. Both refuse rather than downgrade, so an escape attempt is never indistinguishable from a normal request.

The app answers at `<name>.<sites host>`, and its name is claimed in the one namespace app and site names share, first come first served across every org. When another org, app or site holds it, the app takes the first free one of `<name>-<org>`, `<name>-<org>-2` … `-5` instead, and `notice` says so; the same call made again lands on the same app. A `host` named in the request that is taken is 409. Any other host under the sites host is refused, and a custom domain is claimed and verified first.

get.summary: Answers what syncing one app would change.
get.description:
Answers what syncing one app would change.

It reads the CD Application the declaration renders as: the commit CD compared
the cluster against, the commit it last applied, and every object it manages
with CD's verdict on each — the ones that differ from git are what a sync
applies. Object-level, as CD reports it; the field-level diff stays on
cd.hanzo.ai. SuperAdmin only, the same predicate CD's own RBAC applies to
viewing an Application. 404 when CD holds no Application for the declaration.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the declaration's name, from the path.

parameters.name: org
parameters.description:
Org is the values directory the declaration lives in, defaulting to the
caller's own org.

put.summary: Moves an app to a project.
put.description:
Moves an app to a project.

It sets the declaration's `partOf` — in its cluster overlay when the overlay
sets the key, else in its values file — and nothing else. Naming a project
nothing names yet creates it. `org` is the values directory the app lives in;
`mode` as for create.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the declaration's name, from the path.

post.summary: Syncs one app now: CD applies the commit it compared, to this one Application.
post.description:
Syncs one app now: CD applies the commit it compared, to this one
Application.

Every Application is manual — its AppProject admits only a manual sync — so this
is the deploy step, requested the way cd.hanzo.ai requests one: an operation on
the Application, initiated by the caller, applying the compared commit with the
Application's own sync options and no pruning. It answers the Application with
the operation queued; poll the app's cd read for how it ends. SuperAdmin only,
the predicate CD's own RBAC holds sync to, and recorded in the audit trail like
every mutation. 409 while another operation is queued, running or terminating,
before CD has compared the Application with git, and when the Application
changes between the read and the request.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the declaration's name, from the path.

get.summary: Returns real build records for your org.
get.description:
Returns real build records for your org.

It lists the org's BuildKit build records — the git build step behind a deploy —
each with the repo it built, the short commit, its status, when it started and
how long it took, followed by its site builds: a project in the org's own code
workspace built from its repository in a sandbox, newest first. These are real
records or an honest empty list; a build appears here because one ran, never
because a page needed a row. Requires a validated principal; 401 without one.

get.summary: Answers every Application the delivery plane holds.
get.description:
Answers every Application the delivery plane holds.

Scoped to the namespaces the caller's own validated org owns: the ROLE admits
the caller and the tenant boundary is applied inside, so an admin of one org
never observes another's.

get.summary: Returns your deploy targets, and what is running on each.
get.description:
Returns your deploy targets, and what is running on each.

It returns the org's environments — the distinct deploy targets its applications
name, `production` for anything that names none — each aggregating the apps that
target it, a rolled-up status and when it last changed.

An environment is DERIVED, not stored: there is nothing to create or delete here,
and an environment exists exactly as long as an app points at it. Requires a
validated principal; 401 without one.

get.summary: Returns the platform's own service tier, and where it has drifted.
get.description:
Returns the platform's own service tier, and where it has drifted.

It returns the board for the services the PLATFORM itself runs — iam, kms,
gateway and the rest — as `{apps, summary}`: per service its environment, health,
phase, the image tag its CR DECLARES, the tag actually running, and the drift
between them, plus a summary counting the board green, yellow and red.

This is not a customer surface. `/v1/platform/projects/:project/apps` is a
tenant's apps; this is the tier those tenants run ON, which is why the two are
named differently rather than sharing a prefix.

Admission is scoped at the SCAN, before any CR is read: a platform SuperAdmin
observes the whole fleet, an org admin observes only their own org's namespaces,
and an org that owns none gets an empty board — a non-super caller never even
lists another org's services. Narrow further with `env`, `health`, `org`, or
`drift=1` for only what has drifted.

It degrades honestly rather than failing whole: a namespace that does not exist
is skipped, and a running-state read the caller cannot make leaves the running
tag empty — an unknown, never a guess — while the declared, health and phase
columns still render.

parameters.name: env
parameters.description: Env narrows to one lifecycle env: main, test or dev.

parameters.name: health
parameters.description: Health narrows to one health colour: green, yellow or red.

parameters.name: org
parameters.description: Org narrows to one image namespace.

parameters.name: drift
parameters.description:
Drift is `1` or `true` to show only rows that have actually drifted. It is
a STRING and not a bool because those two spellings are exactly what the
board has always accepted, and a bool would silently widen that to `?drift`
alone and to `TRUE` — a behaviour change wearing a type change's clothes.

get.summary: Returns one platform service, resolved to production by default.
get.description:
Returns one platform service, resolved to production by default.

It returns a single platform service by its CR name, with the same
declared-versus-running and drift facts the board carries. The name must be a
DNS-1123 label; anything else is 400.

Namespaces are scanned in lifecycle order — main, then test, then dev — and the
first match wins, so a bare name resolves to PRODUCTION. The scan covers only the
namespaces the caller is authorized for, so an org admin can never read a service
outside their own org, and a name found in none of them is 404 rather than a leak.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the service's CR name, from the path. It must be a DNS-1123 label.

parameters.name: env
parameters.description:
Env narrows the scan to one lifecycle env: main, test or dev. Omitted, the
namespaces are scanned in lifecycle order and the first match wins, so a
bare name resolves to PRODUCTION.

post.summary: Rolls a platform service's pods, in a named environment.
post.description:
Rolls a platform service's pods, in a named environment.

It triggers a rolling restart of one platform service's Deployment by stamping a
fresh restart annotation, and answers 202 with the app, the namespace, the
environment and the timestamp. It restarts pods; it does NOT change the image — a
version change is the release path, not this.

SuperAdmin ONLY, and deliberately narrower than the read gate beside it. The only
namespaces this board touches are the platform's own tier, so a restart here
recycles a SHARED service every tenant depends on. A brand-org admin is a
customer-org admin, not a platform operator: observing the board is bounded and
audited, and restarting production identity is not.

`?env=main|test|dev` is REQUIRED — a bare call does not default to production,
which is what closes the fat-finger and confused-deputy hazard — and any other
value is 400. A service with no Deployment to restart in that environment is 404.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the service's CR name, from the path. It must be a DNS-1123 label.

get.summary: Reports whether this control plane can actually deploy anything.
get.description:
Reports whether this control plane can actually deploy anything.

A real probe, not a status page. It answers 200 only when the metadata store is
open AND the cluster is genuinely reachable — proved by LISTING the operator App
CRD, which settles reachability and CRD presence in one bounded call, and which
is the exact question every deploy depends on. Anything else is 503 carrying the
real reason and whether the CRD was found.

A constructed cluster client proves nothing — it is built from a kubeconfig, not
from a reachable apiserver — so this deliberately spends a round trip rather than
reporting `ok` while every deploy fails. Not admin-gated: liveness has to be
probe-able without a credential.

get.summary: Returns one build-and-deploy pipeline per app, with its latest run.
get.description:
Returns one build-and-deploy pipeline per app, with its latest run.

It returns one pipeline per application in the caller's org — its repo or image
source, its current status, and when its most recent deployment ran and how long
it took. A pipeline is a PROJECTION of an app plus its newest deployment, not a
separate record: it comes into existence with the app and is triggered only
through /deploy, never here. Requires a validated principal; 401 without one.

get.summary: Answers every project the caller may see, with how its apps stand.
get.description:
Answers every project the caller may see, with how its apps
stand.

A project is the `partOf` its apps' values files name, so this is the
declaration inventory grouped by that key, joined per app with CD's
reconciliation, the pods the cluster runs and the newest release the registry
publishes, and folded into counts: apps, namespaces, sync, health and drift.
Declarations that name no project are listed separately, because each one is
drift in git.

A SuperAdmin sees every owner's projects, the platform's own among them; an
org admin sees only its own org's. `org` narrows a SuperAdmin to one owner.
A plane that cannot be read leaves its counts at unknown and says why in
cdUnavailable or clusterUnavailable; it never empties the board. A values file
that does not parse is listed in unreadable and costs only its own row.

parameters.name: org
parameters.description:
Org names whose projects to read. Omitted, a SuperAdmin reads every owner's
and anyone else reads their own; naming another org is an act-as only a
SuperAdmin has, and naming a platform directory reads the platform's own.

post.summary: Creates a project from the apps it starts with.
post.description:
Creates a project from the apps it starts with.

A project is the `partOf` its apps' values files name, so creating one names it
on the listed apps: one commit to `hanzoai/universe` that moves each file's
`partOf` scalar and touches nothing else. There is no empty project; to start
one with a new app, create the app with `partOf` (POST /v1/platform/apps).

`mode` is `branch` (the default: a review branch, nothing deploys) or `commit`
(main). A `partOf` change relabels the app's pods, so the sync that applies it
rolls them. 409 when the name already names apps — move apps into an existing
project with PUT /v1/platform/apps/{app}/project. An org admin changes its own
org's projects; the platform's own, and another org's, are SuperAdmin.

delete.description:
Folds a project into another.

An app always belongs to exactly one project, so a project ends by moving its
apps: `into` names the existing project they move to, and the project is gone
once no file names it. One commit to `hanzoai/universe`; `mode` as for create.
404 when `into` is not a project.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project to delete, from the path.

parameters.name: into
parameters.description:
Into is the existing project its apps move into. Required: an app always
belongs to exactly one project.

parameters.name: org
parameters.description: Org names the projects' owner, defaulting to the caller's own scope.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Mode is `branch` (the default) or `commit`.

get.summary: Answers one project and every app in it.
get.description:
Answers one project and every app in it.

Each app carries its declaration — image, hosts, replicas, the KMS paths it
reads (never a value) — together with the CD Application reconciling it, what
its pods run, the newest release its registry publishes, and the drift between
those four. 404 when no declaration in the caller's scope names the project.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project's name, from the path.

parameters.name: org
parameters.description:
Org names the project's owner, defaulting to the caller's own scope — which
for a SuperAdmin whose home is a brand org is the platform's.

put.description:
Renames a project.

It rewrites `partOf` on every declaration that names the project, in one commit
to `hanzoai/universe`. 409 when the new name is already a project: fold into it
with DELETE /v1/platform/projects/{project}?into=. `mode` as for create.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project to rename, from the path.

get.summary: Returns the applications in one project, with what the cluster says about them.
get.description:
Returns the applications in one project, with what the cluster says
about them.

It lists the caller org's applications under one project. Each row carries the
stored record and, for an app that is live or deploying, the LIVE phase and
health read from its operator Service CR; an app with sealed env also carries
its secret-sync state. Those cluster reads are best-effort — an unreachable
cluster leaves those fields empty and never blocks the listing.

The project must exist in IAM for this org, or the answer is 404; the `default`
project is implicit and always accepted, because it is part of what an org IS.
Requires a validated principal; 401 without one.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project's name, from the path.

post.summary: Creates an application from a git repo or a container image.
post.description:
Creates an application from a git repo or a container image.

It registers a new application under one of the caller org's projects and
answers 201 with it. Creating does NOT deploy: the app lands in `draft` and
nothing reaches the cluster until /deploy.

`source` is `git` — which requires `repo.url` — or `image`, which requires
`image.repository`; anything else is 400. A git app builds with zero-config
`pack` by default and may opt into `dockerfile`; an image app never builds. The
repo URL and Dockerfile path are validated here against the SAME allowlist the
privileged build enforces, so an unsafe source is refused before it is ever
persisted.

The `slug` is the app's identity in the cluster: given or derived from `name`,
it must match `^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]{0,38}[a-z0-9])?$`, and a slug already used in
this project is 409. `replicas` and `storageGb` are clamped to the deployment's
limits rather than refused.

Env keys must match `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`. A variable marked `secret: true`
is SEALED into KMS and its plaintext is never written to the database — and if
KMS is unavailable the create fails 503 rather than falling back to storing a
secret in the clear.

The app is seeded with its canonical default host, so it has a working HTTPS URL
the moment it deploys. A bare custom domain cannot be attached here — it has to
go through add-domain and DNS verification first. Requires a validated
principal; 401 without one, and every cluster object it will later create lands
in that org's own `tenant-<org>` namespace.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project to create the application under, from the path.

delete.summary: Deletes an application and tears down what it runs.
delete.description:
Deletes an application and tears down what it runs.

It removes the application record and tears down what it owns in the org's
tenant namespace — its operator Service CR and its KMSSecret — then answers 204.
An app this org and project do not have is 404, never a silent success.

Teardown is best-effort by design: a cluster that refuses or is unreachable does
not block the delete, so the record cannot be left orphaned behind a broken
cluster; the failure is logged for operators and the orphan reaper reconciles
it. Requires a validated principal; 401 without one.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

get.summary: Returns one application, with its live phase, health and secret sync.
get.description:
Returns one application, with its live phase, health and secret sync.

It returns a single application of the caller's org together with what the
cluster currently reports for it: the operator Service CR's phase and health,
and whether its sealed env has synced. An app this org and project do not have
is 404. Requires a validated principal; 401 without one.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

post.summary: Deploys the app — building it first if it comes from git.
post.description:
Deploys the app — building it first if it comes from git.

It starts a new, monotonically versioned deployment of the app and answers 202
with the deployment record. A 202 is an ACCEPTED deployment, not a live one.

An IMAGE app deploys the tag you name (falling back to the app's tag, then
`latest`) by writing its operator Service CR; the operator reconciles it to
running. A GIT app launches an in-cluster BuildKit Job at `commit` — or the app's
branch — and comes back in `building`; the Service CR is applied later, by the
reconciler, once the Job succeeds. The reconciler is restart-safe, so a build in
flight survives a cloud restart.

Deploys are bounded per org: over the concurrent-deploy cap is 429 and NOTHING is
recorded, so a rejected deploy leaves no phantom in the history. An unreachable
cluster is 503 but still records an honest `error` deployment, because a deploy
that was attempted and failed must not be indistinguishable from one never made.
Every other failure is likewise recorded in its real terminal state.

This is metered work: a git build is billed to the org's ledger in wall-clock
build minutes once the Job finishes, and the running deployment is billed for its
compute per tick for as long as it stays live. Requires a validated principal; 401
without one, and everything is written into that org's own `tenant-<org>`
namespace.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

get.summary: Returns an app's deployment history.
get.description:
Returns an app's deployment history.

It lists every deployment recorded for one of the caller org's applications,
newest version first, each with its version, status, source, commit and image.
Failed and superseded attempts are included — that is the point of a history.
Requires a validated principal; 401 without one.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

get.summary: Returns one deployment of one app.
get.description:
Returns one deployment of one app.

It returns a single deployment by id, scoped to the named application of the
caller's org — so an id belonging to another app or another tenant is 404, not a
read. Requires a validated principal; 401 without one.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: ID is the deployment's id, from the path.

get.summary: Returns real logs for a deployment — the build's, then the app's.
get.description:
Returns real logs for a deployment — the build's, then the app's.

It returns the deployment's recorded status timeline together with LIVE pod logs
pulled from the cluster: the build pod's output while a git build is running, and
the running app's output once it is deployed. The `source` field says which of
the two the body is — `build`, `app` or `none` — so a console can label the pane
honestly.

It never fabricates log content. When no pod exists yet, or the cluster is
unreachable, it degrades to the recorded timeline and says so. Every cluster read
is confined to the caller org's own namespaces and time-boxed. Requires a
validated principal; 401 without one.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: ID is the deployment's id, from the path.

get.summary: Returns every hostname this app answers on.
get.description:
Returns every hostname this app answers on.

It lists the app's hosts: the permanent default host it was born with, and
every custom host claimed for it with its
verification state and, while pending, the DNS challenge records to publish. Live
endpoint status for each host is observed from the cluster. Requires a validated
principal; 401 without one.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

parameters.name: app
parameters.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

post.summary: Attaches a hostname — instantly if you already own it, otherwise with a DNS challenge.
post.description:
Attaches a hostname — instantly if you already own it, otherwise with a
DNS challenge.

It attaches a bring-your-own `host` to the app: the host is claimed as PENDING
and answers 201 with the DNS challenge records to publish. It is NOT rendered
into the app's ingress until /verify passes.

Claims are globally unique. A host already claimed by another organization is
409, and so is one claimed by a different app in your own; re-adding this app's
OWN claim is idempotent and answers its current state at 200. The default host is
always attached and re-adding it is 409. Any other host under the platform's
shared apex is 403: a name there is an app's own, taken when that app was
created, and is never claimed through the custom path.

`host` must be a valid DNS hostname; anything else is 400. Requires a validated
principal; 401 without one.

delete.summary: Detaches a hostname and releases the claim.
delete.description:
Detaches a hostname and releases the claim.

It drops the host from the app's ingress and releases any custom claim on it, so
the name becomes claimable again — by this org or any other. Answers 204.

The default host is permanent and cannot be removed: that is 400, not 404. A host
that is neither attached nor claimed here is 404. Requires a validated principal;
401 without one.

post.summary: Checks a custom domain's DNS and turns it on if it passes.
post.description:
Checks a custom domain's DNS and turns it on if it passes.

It runs the DNS challenge check for a pending custom host and, when it passes,
marks the host verified and renders it into the app's ingress so it starts
serving.

A check that RAN and did not pass is not an error: it answers 200 with the host
still pending and the reason in `detail`, so a console can show the operator what
DNS is actually returning. An already-verified host answers as-is without
re-checking. A host not claimed by this app is 404. Requires a validated
principal; 401 without one.

put.description:
Replaces an app's environment variables.

It writes the app's whole environment set and answers the updated application.
This is the one post-create write path for env, and it REPLACES rather than
merges: a variable absent from the body is gone, and a secret dropped from the
set leaves the app's Secret on its next deploy.

Keys must match `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`. A value marked `secret: true` is
sealed into KMS and blanked in the database, so plaintext is never persisted —
and the write fails 503 if KMS is unavailable rather than storing one in the
clear.

The rule worth knowing: this does not restart anything. Once the app has been
deployed the secret sync is re-declared immediately so the operator
re-materialises the Secret, but RUNNING pods keep the environment they started
with until their next deploy or restart. Requires a validated principal; 401
without one.

post.summary: Puts a branch on its own URL.
post.description:
Puts a branch on its own URL.

It deploys an already-built `image` to a per-branch preview and answers its URL,
the branch, the preview's slug and the deployment. The preview is a FIRST-CLASS
application named `<app>-<branch>` in the same project and tenant namespace, with
its own default host — so it is completely isolated from production while reusing
the same deploy mechanic. Re-previewing a branch converges that same target in
place rather than stacking another one.

It carries NO environment variables, deliberately: a preview never inherits
production's secrets. It also does not build — `image` is required and must
already exist, and `branch` defaults to the parent app's. A branch that does not
resolve to a valid slug distinct from the parent's is 400. Requires a validated
principal; 401 without one.

post.summary: Promotes an already-built release to the app.
post.description:
Promotes an already-built release to the app.

It redeploys an image that already exists — named either by `deploymentId`, which
promotes that deployment's exact built image, or by `tag`, resolved the same way
a deploy resolves one. One of the two is required; neither is 400.

Promotion never builds. A deployment that carries no built image cannot be
promoted and is 400, and a deployment id outside this app is 404. It runs through
the same deploy core as everything else, so it takes a NEW version number and is
subject to the same per-org concurrency cap. Requires a validated principal; 401
without one.

post.summary: Goes back to the previous release.
post.description:
Goes back to the previous release.

It redeploys a prior image: the one named by `deploymentId`, or — with no body —
the newest earlier deployment that carries a real built image and did not error,
skipping the release currently live. An app with nothing earlier to return to is
400.

A rollback is a deploy of an old image, not a rewind: it takes a NEW version
number and appends to the history rather than erasing what came after. Both
lookups are scoped to this app and org, so another tenant's image can never be
rolled in. Requires a validated principal; 401 without one.

post.summary: Starts a stopped app back up.
post.description:
Starts a stopped app back up.

It scales the app's Service back to its configured replica count and marks it
live, answering the updated application. It does not redeploy: the image already
on the Service CR is what comes back.

The billing watermark is reset to now as part of starting, so the org is charged
for THIS live span and never for the gap the app spent stopped. An app with no
Service CR is 404, an unreachable cluster is 503, and a cluster that refuses the
scale is 502. Requires a validated principal; 401 without one.

post.summary: Stops an app without deleting it.
post.description:
Stops an app without deleting it.

It scales the app's Service to zero replicas and marks it stopped, answering the
updated application. Nothing else is removed — the record, its env, its domains
and its deployment history all survive, and /start brings it back at the same
replica count.

An app that is not deployed has no Service CR to scale and is 404. An
unreachable cluster is 503 and a cluster that refuses the scale is 502. Because
the pods stop, so does the compute metering. Requires a validated principal; 401
without one.

get.summary: Returns the versions that actually reached the cluster.
get.description:
Returns the versions that actually reached the cluster.

It lists the org's releases: the deployments that were genuinely applied to the
cluster, with the app they belong to, their version, environment, status and when
they were released. A deployment that failed or is still building is NOT a
release and is excluded — reaching the cluster is what makes one. Requires a
validated principal; 401 without one.

post.summary: Runs a container image and gives back a URL.
post.description:
Runs a container image and gives back a URL.

The one-call shortcut over project → app → deploy: give it a `name` and an
`image` and it creates or updates an image-source application in your org's
DEFAULT project, deploys it through the same operator Service-CR writer
everything else uses, and answers its id, name, live URL, status and shape.
Re-running the same name UPDATES it in place, so the call is idempotent by name.

What it produces is a first-class application, not a special object: it is
listable, stoppable and redeployable through the /v1/platform routes like any
other app.

`minScale` is the replica floor. `maxScale` above it declares an autoscaling
ceiling; `maxScale: 0` means no autoscaler at all — a fixed run at the floor.
Both are clamped to the deployment's limits. `runtime` and `shape` are accepted
for the client contract and echoed back: the image is the runtime unit and sizing
is the operator's default.

It is BILLING-GATED before it touches the cluster: a flat per-run fee is
authorized against the org's own prepaid balance first, so an org that cannot pay
is refused without anything being created. An unreachable cluster is 503 — a run
never reports a URL it did not create. Secret env is sealed into KMS and fails
closed without it.

Requires a validated principal; 401 without one. The org is resolved from that
validated identity and is what both pays and owns the namespace — it is never
read from the body.

cd.automated in the values file, rendered by the ApplicationSet's
templatePatch — false means the Application reports drift and nothing moves.

workload lands. For a fleet Application that is the org, but this is the
OBSERVED field and not our model of it: the two can disagree, and a board

Secrets are the KMS coordinates the app reads — kmsSecrets and secrets.paths

Kind is which finding this is, one of stale, un-rolled, floating-declared,
floating-running, no-release or zero-assets. It is what code matches on, and
the kinds are independent — one row can carry several at once.

message.description:
Message is the finding in words, naming the tags that produced it ("running
v1.2.3 has not rolled to declared v1.2.4"). For display: match on Kind.

Severity is this ONE finding's weight — yellow for stale and un-rolled, red
for the other four. It is a constant of the kind (severityOf), never a

key.description:
Key is the variable's name in the container, which must match

of the KMS ref, so it is what identifies the value across a round trip.

secret.description:
Secret says the value lives in KMS and never in the database. A caller may
only ADD secrecy: the server seals a value whose key or shape looks like a
credential anyway (secretshape.go), so an entry can come back secret that
was not sent that way.

value.description:
Value is the plaintext, and it is WRITE-ONLY once the entry is secret: a
sealed value reads back as "", and sending "" again KEEPS what is sealed
rather than wiping it. Only a non-empty value seals a new one.

floating-declared, floating-running, stale, un-rolled, then the
release-artifact ones. Always present — `[]` for a row that runs what it
declares, never null.

any is yellow, else ok. It is the column a board sorts and filters on, and
"ok" is exactly what no flags means.

buildType.description:
BuildType is how a git app builds: `pack`, the zero-config default that
detects the project, or `dockerfile`. An image app carries `image`, which
means it never builds.

createdAt.description: CreatedAt is when the app was created, unix seconds.

currentDeploymentId.description:
CurrentDeploymentID is the deployment that is live — the pointer a deploy
advances monotonically by version, so it never regresses to an older one.
Empty until the first deploy reaches the cluster.

description.description: Description is free text about what the app is. Nothing derives from it.

dockerfile.description:
Dockerfile is the path inside the repo to build from, for buildType
`dockerfile`. The build path keys off its presence, and it is validated at
create against the same allowlist the privileged build enforces.

domains.description:
Domains are the ingress hosts rendered into the app's CR, its own
`<slug>.<sites host>` first. That one is seeded at create and cannot be
removed; a custom host joins only after add-domain and DNS verification.

env.description:
Env is the app's environment variables, with every SECRET value masked to ""
— the plaintext is in KMS and this surface never echoes it. That masking is
why an empty secret value means "keep what is sealed" when posted back.

environment.description:
Environment is the deploy target this app names, `production` when none was
given. It is a LABEL: /v1/platform/environments derives the environment list
from the apps that name one, so an environment exists as long as an app
points at it and no route creates or deletes one.

health.description:
Health rolls ready-vs-desired replicas up to a colour: green (all ready),
yellow (some ready, or deliberately scaled to zero), red (none), or "" when
the cluster reports no replica counts at all — unknown, never a guessed green.

id.description:
ID is the server-minted application id (`app_…`). Routes address an app by
project and slug; this is the key its deployments and builds carry.

image.description:
Image is the image a source `image` app runs. For a git app only the tag is
filled, stamped by the deploy that went live; the built ref is on the
deployment.

name.description: Name is the display name. It is not an address — the slug is.

namespace.description:
Namespace is where the app's cluster objects live, `tenant-<org>`. It is
derived from the validated org and is never accepted from a request.

org.description:
Org is the tenant that owns the app. It comes from the validated identity,
never from the request, and it is the boundary every route is scoped to.

phase.description:
Phase is the operator's own `status.phase` for the app's Service CR, read
from the cluster on this request. Empty when there is no CR yet or the
cluster could not be read.

port.description:
Port is the container port traffic is sent to. 8080 when the create asked
for none, or for one outside 1–65535.

projectId.description:
ProjectID is the IAM project the app lives under, and it is that project's
NAME — the (org,name) key IAM identifies it by, which is also what the
`:project` path segment carries. There is no platform-minted project id.

replicas.description:
Replicas is how many copies the CR declares. It is CLAMPED to the
deployment's ceiling rather than refused, so it can be below what was asked.

repo.description:
Repo is the git origin a source `git` app builds from, and the repo+branch a
landed push has to match to build it.

secretSync.description:
SecretSync is how far the app's secret env has got into the cluster:
""|pending|syncing|ready|failed (secrets.go). It is best-effort and never
fails a deploy, so `pending` is ordinary right after one.

secretSyncDetail.description:
SecretSyncDetail is the honest reason when the sync is not ready — a missing
CRD, an RBAC grant, a per-tenant credential. Empty when it is.

slug.description:
Slug is the app's identity in the cluster: the operator CR's name, the first
label of its default host, and the `:app` path segment. Unique per project.

source.description:
Source is what the app deploys FROM: `git`, which builds Repo, or `image`,
which runs Image as it is. It decides whether a deploy builds at all.

status.description:
Status is the lifecycle THIS store records: draft (created, nothing in the
cluster yet), building, deploying, live, stopped or error. What the cluster
itself says is Phase and Health.

storageGb.description:
StorageGB is the persistent volume size in GiB. Absent means stateless —
no volume at all — and it is clamped like Replicas.

updatedAt.description:
UpdatedAt is when it last changed, unix seconds. Every lifecycle transition
moves it, so it tracks deploys as well as edits.

image.description:
Image is the toolchain image the recipe runs in, a Go bookworm image by
default. It is the one field the GitHub lane ignores: there the runner IS
the toolchain, and a cluster has to be told what a runner already is.

ldflags.description:
Ldflags are the Go linker flags, `-s -w` when the recipe names none, on one
line. Go lane only.

main.description:
Main is the Go package to build, repo-relative (`.` or `./cmd/x`), and it
selects the GO LANE. Defaults to `.` when neither lane is named; declaring
it together with `run` is refused.

name.description:
Name is the artifact's base name: the prefix of every file published for
this entry, and the name a host later asks for. It must match
`^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}$`, which is what makes it safe as both a
filename and a URL path segment.

out.description:
Out is the glob of files `run` produced, relative to the repo root; matching
nothing FAILS the build rather than publishing an empty entry. It expands
unquoted, so it is bounded to path and glob characters. The Go lane names
its own files and ignores this.

platforms.description:
Platforms are the `<os>/<arch>` pairs the Go lane cross-compiles, [linux/amd64]
by default. Each one publishes as `<name>-<os>-<arch>`, which is the shape a
host resolves a binary BY — so the list is what a caller can ask for later.

run.description:
Run is any other toolchain's build command, run by `sh -c` in this entry's
image, and it selects the OTHER LANE. Arbitrary shell is the point — it is
the same trust as a Dockerfile RUN — which is why it executes with no
object-store credential and no service-account token. It requires `out`.

builds.description: Builds are the org's real BuildKit build records, newest first.

commit.description: Commit is the short git ref the build pinned.

duration.description: Duration is the wall time of a TERMINAL build; empty while it still runs.

id.description: ID is the build record's id.

repo.description: Repo is the repo the build built, or the image it produced.

startedAt.description: StartedAt is when the build was recorded, RFC3339 UTC.

status.description: Status is the build's real state: queued, building, succeeded or failed.

application.description: Application is the CD Application the declaration renders as.

applied.description: Applied is the universe commit CD last synced, "" before its first sync.

compared.description:
Compared is the universe commit CD compared the cluster against — the one
a sync applies.

operation.description: Operation is the phase of a sync in flight or last run, "" when none ran.

pending.description: Pending are the objects that differ from git: what a sync would apply.

resources.description: Resources is every object the Application manages.

sync.description: Sync is CD's verdict: Synced or OutOfSync.

buildType.description:
BuildType is `pack` — the zero-config default that detects any project —
or `dockerfile`, the explicit escape hatch. An image app never builds.

description.description: Description is free text about what the application is.

dockerfile.description: Dockerfile is the path to build from, for buildType `dockerfile`.

domains.description:
Domains are extra ingress hosts. The canonical default host is always
attached; a bare custom host is refused here and must go through
add-domain → verify first.

env.description:
Env is the application's environment. Keys must match
`^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`; a variable marked `secret: true` is sealed into
KMS and its plaintext is never written to the database.

Name is the application's display name. Required; the slug is derived from
it when none is given.

Replicas is how many copies to run; clamped to the deployment's limit
rather than refused.

Slug is the app's identity in the cluster — its CR name and part of its
host. Given or derived from Name, it must match
`^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]{0,38}[a-z0-9])?$`, and one already used in this
project is 409.

source.description:
Source is `git`, which requires repo.url, or `image`, which requires
image.repository. Anything else is 400.

storageGb.description:
StorageGB is the persistent volume size in GiB; absent means stateless.
Clamped to the deployment's limit rather than refused.

name.description: Name is the declaration's name, the file's basename.

org.description: Org is the values directory the declaration lives in.

public.description:
Public marks a value that may be WRITTEN INTO GIT. Absent, it is false,
and the value is sealed into KMS and referenced.

★ THE DEFAULT IS SECRET, AND THE POLARITY IS THE WHOLE DESIGN. This lane's
output is a commit in a repository replicated to every clone, so a value
written there stays there. Sealing by default means the worst outcome of a
wrong guess is a config value an operator reads back from KMS rather than
from git, and nothing sensitive ever depends on recognising its shape.

It is also the only rule that needs no list: a password, a kubeconfig or an
MFA seed is sealed whatever it looks like, because only an explicit public
mark writes a value into git.

application.description:
Application is the CD Application name the generator mints from the path —
the directory joined to the file name, less any words the two share
(applicationName). It is how cd.hanzo.ai names the app.

automated.description:
Automated is cd.automated: false means the Application reports drift and
NOTHING moves. It is off by default for a new file on purpose.

component.description: Component is the app's role within its project (`component`), "" when unnamed.

env.description:
Env is the declared container environment, as the chart's list of
{name,value}. It is read back so a re-declare of an identical body is a
no-op rather than a refusal — idempotency is what makes a retry safe.

name.description: the Helm release name — the file's basename

org.description:
Org is the owner. It is ALSO the values directory and the destination
namespace, because those are one value under one name — see the header.

partOf.description:
PartOf is the platform project this app belongs to: the values file's own
`partOf` key, which the chart also stamps on every object it renders as
app.kubernetes.io/part-of. It is the ONE declaration of membership — there is
no project table — and "" means the file names none.

path.description: Path is the file, relative to the repository root.

project.description:
Project is the AppProject the sync is admitted under, derived from the
directory exactly as the ApplicationSet derives it. It differs from Org
for a reserved directory, which syncs under the platform fence.

secrets.description:
Secrets are the KMS coordinates the app reads — kmsSecrets and secrets.paths
— as paths and key names. A values file never carries a secret value, so
neither does this.

org.description:
Org is the directory read — the caller's own, or another when a SuperAdmin
asked to act as it.

unreadable.description:
Unreadable are the org's values files that do not parse, so they are not
among apps. Absent when every file parsed.

deploymentId.description: DeploymentID is the deployment these logs belong to.

logs.description:
Logs is the recorded status timeline followed by the streamed pod output,
newline-separated.

source.description:
Source says which pod the log body carries — `build`, `app`, or `none` when
neither pod was reachable — so a console can label the pane honestly.

app.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

commit.description:
Commit is the git commit or ref to build, for a git-source app. Defaults to
the app's branch.

project.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

tag.description:
Tag is the image tag to deploy, for an image-source app. Defaults to the
app's tag, then `latest`.

applicationId.description: ApplicationID is the app this deployed — the app's `id`, not its slug.

buildId.description:
BuildID is the build record behind a git deploy, whose logs and status live
at /v1/platform/builds. Empty for an image deploy.

commit.description:
Commit is the git ref this built — the commit a deploy or a push named,
else the app's branch. Empty for an image deploy, which builds nothing.

createdAt.description: CreatedAt is when the attempt was recorded, unix seconds.

id.description:
ID is the deployment's id (`dep_…`), minted when the attempt is recorded.
The app's currentDeploymentId points at one of these.

image.description:
Image is the full `repo:tag` this deployment put in the CR. For a git deploy
it is the ref the in-cluster build pushes to, known before the build runs.

message.description:
Message is why this attempt is not live: the failure, or the note that a
newer deployment went live before this build finished. Empty while it is fine.

org.description: Org is the tenant the deployment belongs to, from the validated identity.

source.description:
Source is which lane produced it: `git` (built from the repo) or `image`
(an already-built ref deployed as-is, including promote and rollback).

status.description:
Status is where the attempt got to: `building` while its image is being
built, `deploying` once its CR reached the cluster — which is the terminal
success state, the app's own status is what turns `live` — `error` with the
reason in Message, or `superseded` when a newer version went live first.

updatedAt.description:
UpdatedAt is its last transition, unix seconds — so for a terminal
deployment it is when it reached that state.

version.description:
Version counts this app's deployments, from 1 and monotonically. It is what
ORDERS them: a deploy only goes live if no higher version already is, so a
build that finishes late is superseded instead of overwriting a newer one.

createdAt.description: CreatedAt is the unix second the custom claim was made.

detail.description: Detail says why a claim is still pending, in the resolver's own words.

kind.description:
Kind is `default` (the app's own name) or `custom` — how the org came to
own it.

primary.description: Primary marks the app's permanent default host.

records.description: Records are the DNS records to publish while a custom claim is pending.

status.description:
Status is `live`, `provisioning`, `pending_deploy` or `pending`, derived
from the operator CR and never fabricated.

url.description: URL is the host as an HTTPS address.

verified.description:
Verified is whether ownership is settled — always true for a host the org
structurally owns.

apps.description: Apps are the service rows, ordered by org, then app, then env.

summary.description: Summary counts the board by drift severity.

ok.description: OK is how many rows run what they declare.

red.description: Red is how many have drifted badly.

yellow.description: Yellow is how many have drifted within tolerance.

environments.description: Environments are the org's deploy targets, in first-seen order.

id.description:
ID is the environment's name, which is also its identity — an environment
is derived from the apps that target it, so it has no id of its own.

name.description: Name is the environment's name as an app declared it.

services.description: Services are the apps that target this environment, by name.

status.description:
Status rolls up the real states of this environment's apps: degraded,
active, idle or empty.

type.description:
Type buckets the name for display: production, staging, development or
custom.

updatedAt.description: UpdatedAt is when any of them last changed, RFC3339 UTC; empty when unset.

byDrift.description: ByDrift counts those rows green, yellow and red.

total.description: Total is how many rows the board returned, after filtering.

branch.description: Branch is the branch to build; defaults to `main` for a git source.

url.description:
URL is the repository clone URL. Required for source `git`, and validated
against the same allowlist the privileged build enforces.

branch.description:
Branch is the branch a push-to-deploy build tracks, `main` when the create
named none — a push to any other branch, and every tag push, builds nothing
here. A deploy may name a commit instead, for that deploy alone.

provider.description:
Provider is derived from the URL — github, gitlab, bitbucket, or `git` for
anything else. It is a label for display; no behaviour keys on it.

url.description:
URL is the clone URL a git app builds from, stored as sent once the build
path's allowlist accepted it (validateRepoURL). It is also what a landed
push is MATCHED against, so a push to any other repo never builds this app.

degraded.description: Degraded is how many CD reports Degraded.

healthy.description: Healthy is how many CD reports Healthy.

missing.description: Missing is how many have no live objects at all.

progressing.description: Progressing is how many are still rolling out.

unknown.description: Unknown is every other verdict, and apps CD could not be asked about.

repository.description: Repository is the image repository. Required for source `image`.

tag.description: Tag is the image tag to deploy; `latest` when omitted.

repository.description:
Repository is the image path without a tag (ghcr.io/acme/api). Required for
source `image`, which runs it as-is. A git app's built image is NOT this: the
build pushes to a path derived from the org and slug, and the deployment
records that full ref.

tag.description:
Tag is the tag to run: what the create declared, then RE-STAMPED on every
transition to live with the tag that actually went live. So after a deploy
it names what is running, not what was asked for.

pipelines.description: Pipelines are one per application in the caller's org.

duration.description:
Duration is how long that run took; empty while it is still queued or
building.

id.description: ID is the application id — one pipeline is one application.

lastRun.description: LastRun is when the most recent deployment started, RFC3339 UTC.

repo.description: Repo is the git repo or image the pipeline builds from.

status.description: Status is the latest deployment's status, or the app's when it has none.

app.description: App is the parent application's slug, from the path.

branch.description: Branch is the branch to preview; defaults to the parent app's branch.

image.description:
Image is the already-built image ref to deploy. Required — a preview never
builds.

project.description: Project is the project the parent application lives under, from the path.

app.description: App is the preview application's own slug, `<app>-<branch>`.

branch.description: Branch is the branch this preview maps.

deployment.description: Deployment is the deployment the preview recorded.

url.description: URL is the preview's live HTTPS address.

cdUnavailable.description: CD says why the reconciliation columns are missing, when they are.

clusterUnavailable.description: Cluster says why the running columns are missing, when they are.

projects.description: Projects are sorted by owner, then name.

unassigned.description:
Unassigned are declarations that name no project. Every declaration names
one, so a non-empty list is drift in git itself.

unreadable.description:
Unreadable are the values files in the caller's scope that do not parse, so
their projects are unknown. Absent when every file parsed.

apps.description:
Apps are the declarations it starts with, each by values directory (`org`,
defaulting to the caller's own) and name. At least one: a project is the apps
that name it.

mode.description:
Mode is `branch` (the default: a review branch, nothing deploys) or `commit`
(main).

name.description: Name is the project, a DNS-1123 label; it becomes each app's `partOf`.

org.description:
Org names the project's owner, defaulting to the caller's own scope; naming
another is an act-as only a SuperAdmin has.

name.description: Name is its new name, which no app may already name.

org.description: Org names the project's owner, defaulting to the caller's own scope.

project.description: Project is the project to rename, from the path.

apps.description: Apps is how many declarations name the project.

cdUnavailable.description: CD says why the reconciliation columns are missing, when they are.

clusterUnavailable.description: Cluster says why the running columns are missing, when they are.

drift.description: Drift counts its apps by drift severity.

health.description: Health counts its apps by CD's health verdict.

members.description: Members are the project's apps, sorted by namespace then name.

name.description: Name is the project, as the values files spell it in `partOf`.

namespaces.description: Namespaces are the namespaces its apps deploy into, sorted.

org.description:
Org is the organization that owns the project. Absent for the platform's own
projects, whose apps live in the platform's directories.

sync.description: Sync counts its apps by CD's sync verdict.

unreadable.description:
Unreadable are the values files in the owner's scope that do not parse, any
of which may name this project. Absent when every file parsed.

commit.description: Commit is the sha the change created, "" when nothing had to move.

live.description: Live says whether the generator will see it: true only on main.

mode.description: Mode is branch (a review; nothing deploys) or commit (main).

moved.description: Moved are the declarations whose partOf moved, and from what.

project.description: Project is the project the change leaves the moved apps in.

ref.description: Ref is the branch the change was pushed to, main for a commit.

review.description: Review is where to open the pull request for a branch.

app.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

deploymentId.description:
DeploymentID promotes that deployment's exact built image. One of this and
Tag is required.

project.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

tag.description: Tag promotes an image tag, resolved the same way a deploy resolves one.

crd.description:
CRD is whether the operator App CRD was found, and is absent when no
cluster client resolved and the question could not be asked.

error.description: Error is the real reason the plane is degraded; absent when it is not.

k8s.description: K8s is whether a cluster client resolved at all. False means no kubeconfig.

service.description: Service is always "platform" — which control plane answered.

status.description: Status is "ok" when this plane can deploy, "degraded" when it cannot.

releases.description: Releases are the deployments that genuinely reached the cluster.

environment.description: Environment is the deploy target the application names.

id.description:
ID is the deployment's id — a release IS a deployment that reached the
cluster.

name.description: Name is the application the release belongs to.

releasedAt.description: ReleasedAt is when the deployment last changed, RFC3339 UTC.

status.description: Status is deploying or live — the two states that mean released.

version.description: Version is the released image tag, or v<n> when the image carries none.

app.description: App is the service's CR name, from the path. It must be a DNS-1123 label.

env.description:
Env is REQUIRED and must be main, test or dev. A bare call does not default
to production, which is what closes the fat-finger and confused-deputy
hazard.

It carries no `validate:"required"`: the handler already refuses an empty env
with the sentence that names the three values, and a validator tag would
replace that sentence with a generic one. The requirement is stated here and
enforced there, once.

app.description: App is the service that was restarted.

env.description: Env is that namespace's lifecycle env.

namespace.description: Namespace is the namespace its Deployment was patched in.

ok.description: OK is always true — a failure is an error, not a false here.

restartedAt.description: RestartedAt is the timestamp stamped onto the pod template, RFC3339 UTC.

app.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

deploymentId.description:
DeploymentID is the deployment to redeploy. Omit it to return to the
previous release.

project.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

env.description:
Env is the run's environment. Keys must match `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`;
a variable marked `secret: true` is sealed into KMS.

gpu.description: GPU is how many GPUs the run asks for; a negative value is 400.

image.description: Image is the container image to run. Required.

maxScale.description:
MaxScale above the floor declares an autoscaling ceiling; 0 means no
autoscaler at all — a fixed run at the floor.

minScale.description: MinScale is the replica floor, clamped to the deployment's limit.

name.description:
Name is the run's name, and the slug is derived from it. Required, and it
must resolve to `^[a-z0-9]([a-z0-9-]{0,38}[a-z0-9])?$`. Re-running the same
name updates that run in place.

port.description: Port is the container port the run listens on.

runtime.description:
Runtime is accepted for the client contract and echoed nowhere: the image
IS the runtime unit.

shape.description:
Shape is a compute size label, echoed back; sizing is the operator's
default. Defaults to "auto".

id.description: ID is the application id the run created or converged.

name.description: Name is the run's name, as stored.

shape.description: Shape is the compute size label the request asked for, or "auto".

status.description: Status is the application's state — `deploying` on a fresh accept.

url.description: URL is the run's live HTTPS address.

log.description:
Log is the build's output, each container under a line naming it, in the
order the pod ran them. A build across several architectures is one Job per
architecture and then the index that joins them, and each is read in that
order under a line naming the Job. Empty when there is no pod to read: the
build is not yet placed, its pods were reaped when their TTL elapsed, or the
cluster cannot be reached. Never a log nobody wrote.

status.description:
Status is the build's recorded status: `queued` or `building` until it
finishes, then `succeeded` or `failed`.

truncated.description:
Truncated is whether a Job's log was cut to its most recent bytes, which its
first line then says too. Each container is read to the tail of its lines
either way, and that cut is not marked.

arch.description: Arch is the target architecture for the artifact lane.

args.description:
Args are --build-arg values. They are what lets several images off ONE
Dockerfile mean different things — the sandbox classes are three entries
differing only by STAGE. Validated at the k8s choke point, with VERSION and
REVISION taking precedence: those are receipts the builder derives from the
tag and the commit, and a caller that could overwrite them could make an
image lie about which commit it is.

binaries.description:
Binaries selects the ARTIFACT lane (artifact.go): build what the repo's
hanzo.yml `binaries:` block declares — a Go binary, an npm tarball, a Rust
binary — and publish it to hanzoai/s3 instead of pushing an image. It is the
same recipe hanzoai/ci reads, sent verbatim, so `image` is meaningless here
and must be absent.

branch.description: Branch is the branch to build when no SHA or Ref is given.

bucket.description: Bucket mirrors hanzo.yml's `bucket:` — where the artifact lane publishes.

context.description: Context is the build context path within the repo.

dockerTarget.description: DockerTarget is the multi-stage build target to stop at.

dockerfile.description: Dockerfile is the path to build from; empty uses the zero-config frontend.

image.description:
Image is the output image ref to push. Required on the image lane, and it
must target a registry namespace the caller's org owns.

os.description: OS is the target operating system for the artifact lane.

platforms.description:
Platforms are the `<os>/<arch>` pairs the image is built for. EMPTY MEANS
EVERY ARCHITECTURE THE FLEET HAS — each built on a node of that
architecture, joined by ONE manifest index, so a single tag serves both.
Name one to build only that one.

ref.description: Ref is the git ref to build when no SHA is given.

repo.description: Repo is the repository clone URL to build. Required on the image lane.

sha.description: SHA is the commit to pin; it wins over Ref and Branch.

tag.description:
Tag is the publish path segment, so both entry points write ONE index at ONE
URL. It defaults to the pinned ref, and must be named explicitly for a
branch.

tags.description:
Tags are more tags of Image's own repository, pushed onto the same manifest
by the same export, so every one names the digest Image does — by
construction, not by a second push agreeing with the first. Bare tags
(`v1.2.3`, `latest`), at most 8, and only beside a tag Image: a digest names
an image that already exists. Duplicates and Image's own tag are dropped;
the answer's `tags` lists what will be written.

buildJobId.description: BuildJobID is the queued build's id, and what its progress is read by.

digest.description:
Digest is the pushed OCI manifest or index digest (`sha256:...`), populated
once the build succeeds so callers can pin private and public images without
a separate GHCR read:packages credential.

image.description: Image is the ref the image lane will push.

index.description: Index is the binaries.json URL the artifact lane will publish.

platforms.description: Platforms are the architectures the image lane will publish, echoed back.

position.description:
Position is the build's place in line while it is `queued`, from 1: how many
builds start before it, and it, were nothing to finish meanwhile. Absent once it runs.

reason.description:
Reason is why a failed build failed, as the cluster said it: the solve's
error line (`error: failed to solve: ...`), a container waiting on what it
cannot have, or the deadline.

runnerPool.description: RunnerPool is the runner class the build was placed on.

status.description:
Status is `queued` while the build waits its turn, `building` once it runs, then
`succeeded` or `failed`. The POST answers `queued`: a build that is accepted has
not run. A build is never refused for the others running.

tags.description:
Tags are the extra tags the image lane will write beside Image, onto the
same manifest: the request's, deduplicated. This is the promise — a tag
absent here will not be written.

target.description: Target is the multi-stage build target, echoed back.

app.description: App is the application's slug, from the path.

env.description:
Env is the app's whole environment set, REPLACING what it had. Keys must
match `^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`; a variable marked `secret: true` is
sealed into KMS and blanked in the database.

project.description: Project is the project the application lives under, from the path.

outOfSync.description: OutOfSync is how many differ from git until someone syncs them.

synced.description: Synced is how many run what git declares.

unknown.description: Unknown is how many CD holds no verdict for, or could not be read.

reason.description: Reason is why: the cause for a SuperAdmin, and which plane for anyone else.

path.description: Path is the values file, relative to the repository root.

reason.description:
Reason is why it could not be read. A SuperAdmin reads the parser's own
words; anyone else reads that it does not parse, because those words can
name the platform's cluster overlay.

code.description: A stable token a client can branch on, when the refusal names one.

detail.description: What was refused, for a person to read.

bearer.description: The caller's credential, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. It is either an access token minted by Hanzo IAM or an API key (pk-/sk-). X-Authorization, and HTTP Basic carrying the token as the password, are accepted spellings of the same header for clients that cannot set Authorization; a browser presents the session cookie instead. Every operation requires it unless it says `security: []`.
